questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with a 4-month history of small, red-brown papules on his trunk and arms. On examination, each papule is topped with a characteristic mica-like scale that, when gently scraped away, reveals a shining brown surface beneath. The lesions are asymptomatic and show no scarring. Which immunological cell type predominantly mediates the tissue inflammation in this condition?
opts: CD8+ cytotoxic T-cells
CD4+ helper T-cells
B-cells producing pathogenic autoantibodies
Neutrophils in response to circulating immune complexes
questions.exp: Pityriasis Lichenoides Chronica (PLC) is mediated by CD4+ helper T-cells, unlike its acute counterpart (PLEVA) which is predominantly CD8+ driven. Some of these T-cells express FoxP3, indicating a regulatory phenotype that explains the more indolent chronic course. PLC is not autoimmune and has no pathogenic autoantibodies.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine FOUR (CD4) golden HELPER knights protecting the castle's treasury of CHRONIC peace, while EIGHT (CD8) red assassins stormed the ACUTE tower next door.

questions.q: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the dermatology clinic with a mixture of comedones and inflammatory lesions on her face. Her parents deny any recent skin trauma or medication use. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
opts: Prescribe topical benzoyl peroxide and reassure parents that this is normal preadolescent acne
Initiate oral isotretinoin therapy given the patient's young age and presence of inflammatory lesions
Refer for urgent endocrine evaluation to exclude severe hyperandrogenism, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, or androgen-secreting tumor
Recommend dietary modifications and increased sun exposure to naturally resolve the acne
questions.exp: Mid-childhood acne (ages 1–7 years) is extremely rare because gonadal and adrenal androgen production is quiescent during this period. The presence of acne in this age group is a major clinical red flag demanding immediate endocrine evaluation to rule out serious pathology such as hyperandrogenism, premature adrenarche, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, or an androgen-secreting tumor.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: A 4-YEAR-OLD with acne is like finding a DRAGON in a NURSERY—it should NOT be there! The quiet hormonal castle (1–7 years) has suddenly awakened, demanding the ENDOCRINE GUARDS to investigate for hidden tumors or adrenal rebels.

questions.q: According to the IADVL Task Force, what is the minimum duration of stability required before considering surgical intervention for vitiligo?
opts: No new lesions for 6 months without Koebner phenomenon
No new lesions, no extension of pre-existing lesions, and absence of Koebner phenomenon for at least 1 year
Stable disease for 3 months as confirmed by VIDA score of +1
Negative Koebner test and minigrafting test positive within 2 months
questions.exp: The IADVL Task Force defines stability as no new lesions, no extension of pre-existing lesions, and absence of Koebner phenomenon for at least 1 year. This stringent criterion is the most critical prerequisite before vitiligo surgery to prevent Koebner phenomenon-induced graft failure. Only patients meeting this 1-year stability window are appropriate candidates for surgical intervention.

questions.q: Which of the following histological findings would most reliably distinguish classic Pityriasis Lichenoides Chronica from Pityriasis Lichenoides Varioliformis Acuta (PLEVA)?
opts: Presence of perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate in the superficial dermis
Marked epidermal necrosis with severe basal vacuolization and massive erythrocyte extravasation
Focal, compact parakeratosis with lymphocyte exocytosis forming pseudo-Munro abscesses
Vacuolar interface dermatitis without significant epidermal necrosis
questions.exp: PLC shows milder histology than PLEVA, featuring vacuolar interface dermatitis, focal parakeratosis, and pseudo-Munro abscesses, but crucially lacks the severe epidermal necrosis, intense basal vacuolization, and massive erythrocyte extravasation seen in PLEVA. This histological mildness correlates with the chronic, indolent clinical course and absence of scarring in PLC.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: The CHRONIC castle has a gentle VACUUM (vacuolar) tunnel and soft PARAKERATOTIC walls, while the ACUTE fortress next door has MASSIVE BLEEDING CARNAGE with dying tissue everywhere.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with multiple 3-4 mm pearly-white dome-shaped papules with central umbilication on the trunk and arms. Genotyping of the molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV) isolated from the lesions reveals MCV-1. Which statement best reflects the epidemiological significance of this finding?
opts: MCV-1 is rare in children and typically accounts for <10% of childhood infections worldwide
MCV-1 is the dominant subtype responsible for 76-98% of childhood molluscum contagiosum globally
MCV-1 is predominantly sexually transmitted and found in immunosuppressed adults
MCV-1 and MCV-2 have identical genotypes but different clinical presentations
questions.exp: MCV-1 is the most prevalent subtype worldwide, accounting for 76-97% of childhood infections globally and up to 98% of cases in the United States, making it the expected finding in this typical pediatric presentation. MCV-2, by contrast, is more common in adults and immunocompromised hosts, particularly in HIV-positive patients where it accounts for up to 60% of infections.
questions.mnemonic: 🏰 Palace: A CHILD sits on a THRONE holding 76-98 GOLDEN ORBS (MCV-1 percentage), while an ADULT with a WEAKENED SHIELD stands in the shadows holding 60% DARK ORBS (MCV-2 in HIV) — a hierarchy of viral kingdoms.

questions.q: A patient experiences significant pain during local anesthetic injection. Which mechanism best explains why applying vibration near the injection site reduces this pain?
opts: Vibration increases blood flow, improving local anesthetic diffusion and onset
The vibration stimulus travels via fast A-beta fibers, which override slower pain signals via A-delta and C fibers in the dorsal horn (Gate Control Theory)
Vibration causes temporary anesthesia of the skin surface by disrupting nerve conduction
The vibration distracts the patient's attention, preventing conscious perception of pain
questions.exp: The Gate Control Theory explains that vibration/tactile stimuli travel via fast, large myelinated A-beta fibers, which 'close the gate' on pain signals traveling via slower A-delta and C fibers in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. This competitive inhibition at the spinal cord level reduces pain transmission to the brain.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: FAST BETA KNIGHTS on HUGE HORSES gallop through the castle GATE, SLAMMING it shut before SLOW PAIN PEASANTS (A-delta/C fibers) can enter the throne room—vibration = gate slammer!

questions.q: A 45-year-old patient presents with severe hyperkeratosis of the palms and thick psoriatic plaques on the elbows. Which concentration of urea would be most appropriate for initial treatment of the hyperkeratotic areas?
opts: 2–10% urea as a humectant and emollient
10–30% urea for keratolytic effect and desquamation
40–50% urea for immediate nail avulsion
5% urea with occlusion for maintenance therapy
questions.exp: Medium concentration urea (10–30%) combines both humectant properties and keratolytic action through protein breakdown in the stratum corneum, making it ideal for hyperkeratosis and psoriatic plaques. Low concentrations lack sufficient keratolytic power for thick plaques, while high concentrations are reserved for nail disorders and severe cases requiring professional guidance. 🏰 Palace: Imagine a MEDIUM-STRENGTH UREA SOLDIER (20–30%) breaking down the CASTLE'S THICK STONE WALLS (hyperkeratosis) while keeping them moist—not too weak like a squire, not too strong like a cannon.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male of Jewish descent presents with widespread, extremely pruritic discoid lesions that rapidly alternate between weeping and lichenoid phases over the past 18 months. Which of the following statements best characterizes this clinical entity?
opts: It typically affects young women with atopic history and occurs on the hands
It is also called Oid-oid disease and usually resolves spontaneously after a chronic course
It presents with minimal itching and scattered microvesicles on the palms and soles
It is the most common variant of nummular eczema affecting the pediatric population
questions.exp:
Exudative discoid and lichenoid chronic dermatosis (Sulzberger-Garbe syndrome or Oid-oid disease) is a distinctive variant that occurs almost exclusively in adult males of Jewish ancestry aged 40–60 years, presenting with widespread, highly pruritic discoid lesions alternating between exudative and lichenoid phases, typically resolving spontaneously after months to years of chronic course.
🏰 Palace: Imagine a JEWISH GENTLEMAN (40–60 years old) in a castle throne room SWITCHING between SOAKING WET CUSHIONS and HARD LEATHER CHAIRS (exudative–lichenoid alternation), finally finding peace when the curse lifts spontaneously.

questions.q: A 7-year-old girl presents with sharply demarcated, symmetrically distributed erythematous plaques on her extensor surfaces with loosely adherent silvery-white scales. Removal of the scales reveals pinpoint bleeding. Which of the following histological findings is PATHOGNOMONIC for this diagnosis?
opts: Munro microabscesses and Spongiform pustules of Kogoj
Absent granular layer with hyperkeratosis and acanthosis
Dilated, tortuous capillaries in the dermal papillae only
Epidermal spongiosis with eosinophilic infiltration
questions.exp: Munro microabscesses (localized neutrophil collections in the stratum corneum) and Spongiform pustules of Kogoj (neutrophils in the upper spinous layer) are the absolute pathognomonic histological features of plaque psoriasis. While absent granular layer and dilated capillaries are present, the neutrophilic microabscesses are the definitively diagnostic findings.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Two armies of NEUTROPHILS (MUNRO's Microabscesses and KOGOJ's Spongiform pustules) guard the castle's outer walls—one at the corneum gate, one at the spinous tower—making them the ONLY absolute signatures of the psoriasis fortress.

questions.q: A 3-week-old male neonate presents with multiple small erythematous papules and pustules on his cheeks and forehead. The mother is concerned about permanent scarring. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis and key distinguishing histological feature?
opts: Neonatal acne (cephalic pustulosis); characterized by comedonal follicular plugging
Neonatal acne (cephalic pustulosis); non-comedonal pustular inflammatory eruption without true comedones
Infantile acne; predominantly comedonal lesions with sebaceous gland hyperplasia
Preadolescent acne; localized to the T-zone with adrenal androgen stimulation
questions.exp: Neonatal acne peaks at 2–3 weeks and affects >20% of healthy term newborns. It is driven by Malassezia colonization and transiently elevated neonatal androgens. Crucially, it lacks true comedones and shows non-comedonal pustular inflammation on histology, distinguishing it from infantile and other true acne forms. It is self-limiting and resolves without scarring within 1–3 months.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Picture a NEWBORN BABY (0–8 weeks) sitting in a castle nursery covered in PUSTULES but NO COMEDONES—it's like a MALASSEZIA FUNGAL PARTY with temporary inflammation that clears like morning dew, never leaving scars.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man has a 15 mm nodular lesion on the nose clinically suspicious for BCC. The patient desires cosmetic preservation. What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic approach?
opts: Excisional biopsy with 5 mm margins immediately
Shave biopsy to confirm diagnosis, then re-excise with appropriate margins
Incisional biopsy to diagnose, followed by planned wide excision
Punch biopsy from the center of the lesion
questions.exp: Shave biopsy is acceptable for suspected low-risk BCC to establish diagnosis while preserving cosmesis, followed by planned re-excision with appropriate margins if confirmed. Excisional biopsy can be performed but shave avoids unnecessary tissue removal initially. Incisional biopsy leaves tumor behind requiring additional surgery. Punch biopsy alone is too small for complete assessment of a 15 mm lesion.

questions.q: A mother asks about the inheritance pattern and prevalence of Harlequin ichthyosis after delivering an affected neonate. Which statement accurately reflects the epidemiological and genetic characteristics of this condition?
opts: Autosomal dominant inheritance with HLA associations; prevalence ~1 in 50,000 births
Autosomal recessive inheritance with no HLA associations; prevalence ~1 in 2 million births
X-linked recessive inheritance affecting predominantly males; prevalence ~1 in 100,000 births
Autosomal recessive inheritance with strong HLA-B27 association; prevalence ~1 in 500,000 births
questions.exp: Harlequin ichthyosis is a Mendelian autosomal recessive monogenic disorder with an estimated prevalence of approximately 1 in 2 million births. Because it is monogenic, there are no known HLA associations. It exhibits equal sex distribution and occurs in all racial and ethnic groups worldwide, with affected infants frequently born prematurely at a mean gestational age of 35 weeks.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Two recessive SUIT OF ARMOR tokens must BOTH be surrendered to the castle gate (autosomal recessive)—HLA sentries are NOT posted there—and this armor is so rare that only ONE baby in TWO MILLION castles receives it, arriving 5 weeks EARLY to the royal nursery.

questions.q: A premature neonate presents with an armor-like shell of yellow-brown hyperkeratotic plates separated by diamond-shaped bright-red fissures, severe ectropion, eclabium, and mitten-like hand deformities. Electron microscopy shows abnormal, empty lamellar bodies in the stratum granulosum with absence of extracellular lipid lamellae. Which gene mutation is most likely responsible for this presentation?
opts: KDSR gene mutation
ABCA12 gene mutation
FLG gene mutation
TGM1 gene mutation
questions.exp: Classic Harlequin ichthyosis is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the ABCA12 gene in >93% of cases. ABCA12 encodes an ATP-binding cassette lipid transporter that loads lamellar bodies with essential lipids and proteolytic enzymes; its failure prevents intercellular lipid bilayer formation in the stratum corneum. The pathognomonic ultrastructural finding of abnormal or missing lamellar bodies is diagnostic of ABCA12-related disease.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine ARMOR PLATING (ABCA12) being loaded into LAMELLAR BODY WAREHOUSES deep in the castle dungeons—when the ABC transporter gates SLAM SHUT, the lipid cargo never arrives and the fortress skin crumbles into diamond fissures like a shattered stained-glass window.

questions.q: A 2-day-old premature neonate is born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid and presents with lethargy, hepatosplenomegaly, and a generalized eruption of 1–2 mm grey-white papules and pustules with red margins on the back. The mother had no prenatal care. Which of the following best describes the pathological finding on skin biopsy?
opts: Subcorneal acantholysis with IgG autoantibodies against desmoglein 1
Focal tissue necrosis, marked neutrophilic infiltrates, and monocytes clustered around dermal blood vessels
Granulomatous inflammation with caseating necrosis and acid-fast bacilli
Subepidermal blister with linear IgA deposits along the basement membrane zone
questions.exp: Early-onset neonatal listeriosis (granulomatosis infantiseptica) presents with characteristic 1–2 mm grey-white pustules and papules with red margins, typically on the back. Histopathology shows focal necrosis, neutrophilic infiltrates, and monocyte clustering around dermal blood vessels, reflecting blood-borne dissemination in utero. The condition results from transplacental infection by Listeria monocytogenes, not autoimmune or genetic mechanisms.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a GREY-WHITE GHOST (1–2 mm pustules) haunting the BACK HALLWAY of the castle, surrounded by RED MOAT GUARDS (red margin), with NEUTROPHIL KNIGHTS clustering around the BLOOD VESSEL TOWERS like mourners at a funeral (monocyte infiltration).

questions.q: A 7-year-old child presents with sharply demarcated, coin-shaped plaques measuring 1–3 cm on the trunk and extremities. The lesions are dull red, highly pruritic, and show prominent weeping with heavy crust formation. Histology reveals acute spongiotic dermatitis with intercellular edema primarily affecting the basal layer and upper dermis. Which variant of nummular eczema is most consistent with this presentation?
opts: Dry nummular dermatitis
Exudative nummular dermatitis
Nummular dermatitis of the hands
Exudative discoid and lichenoid chronic dermatosis
questions.exp:
Exudative nummular dermatitis is the classic and most common morphological presentation, characterized by dull red, sharply demarcated coin-shaped plaques (1–3 cm) with prominent weeping, crust formation, and intense pruritus. Histologically, it shows acute spongiotic dermatitis with intercellular edema and spongiotic vesicles in the epidermis and upper dermis, with a lymphohistiocytic infiltrate and eosinophils.
🏰 Palace: Picture a COIN-SHAPED CASTLE MOAT (exudative nummular) WEEPING WATER and oozing mud, with soldiers (spongiotic edema) marching in single-file through the basal layer trenches.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with multiple painful vesicles and ulcers on her vulva accompanied by severe pain, dysuria, and bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. The lesions appeared acutely 3 days ago. What is the most likely causative organism?
opts: Treponema pallidum
Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV-1 or HSV-2)
Haemophilus ducreyi
Klebsiella granulomatis
questions.exp: HSV is the most common cause of painful genital ulcers globally and typically presents with acute vesicles progressing to painful erosions with systemic symptoms and lymphadenopathy. The other organisms are either painless (Treponema pallidum, Klebsiella granulomatis) or present with ragged, undermined edges (Haemophilus ducreyi).
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: A HERPETIC VAMPIRE (HSV) throws PAINFUL DARTS into a castle chamber, while a SYPHILITIC GHOST silently wanders the halls without pain.

questions.q: A 3-day-old Black neonate has a large, ill-defined blue-grey patch over the lumbosacral region that parents are concerned may be a bruise from birth trauma. Histology shows melanocytes retained deep within the dermis. What optical phenomenon accounts for the characteristic blue-grey colour?
opts: Oxyhemoglobin in superficial vessels causing cyanosis
Tyndall effect—deep dermal melanin absorbs longer wavelengths and reflects shorter blue/violet wavelengths
Deposition of hemosiderin and lipofuscin in dermal macrophages
Incomplete melanin granule maturation causing light scattering at the dermoepidermal junction
questions.exp: Mongolian spots (congenital dermal melanocytosis) appear blue-grey due to the Tyndall effect: melanocytes are ectopically retained deep in the dermis (having failed to migrate to the dermoepidermal junction during embryogenesis), and deep melanin absorbs longer wavelengths while reflecting shorter blue/violet wavelengths. This is benign and present in 90–100% of Asian and Black neonates.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 1] Physiological, Pigmentary and Mechanical Neonatal Lesions

questions.q: A 45-year-old patient presents with a common wart on the dorsal hand. After discussing treatment options, you decide to use cryotherapy. Which cryogen would be most appropriate for this benign lesion, and why?
opts: Liquid nitrogen, because it achieves the lowest temperature and ensures complete destruction of the lesion
Nitrous oxide, because it is equally effective as liquid nitrogen but safer for benign lesions
DMEP (dimethyl ether and propane), because it is adequate for superficial benign lesions and more convenient than liquid nitrogen
Argon gas, because it is specifically designed for dermatologic surface lesions
questions.exp: DMEP achieves -50°C to -57°C and clinical trials show it is significantly less effective than liquid nitrogen, making it suitable only for superficial benign lesions. While liquid nitrogen is the gold standard, DMEP offers adequate efficacy with convenience for simple benign warts. Nitrous oxide is less effective than liquid nitrogen, and argon gas is reserved for internal cryoablation of deep tumors.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: A WART sits on a SHALLOW SHELF in the castle—it only needs a COLD BREEZE (DMEP at -50°C), not a FREEZING BLIZZARD (LN₂ at -196°C) to blow it away.

questions.q: According to the Gilliam classification, which histopathologic feature is CHARACTERISTIC of LE-specific skin disease?
opts: Perivascular lymphocytic infiltration
Interface dermatitis
Follicular plugging
Spongiosis with neutrophilic microabscesses
questions.exp: James N. Gilliam's classification divides LE skin lesions into LE-specific disease (demonstrating characteristic interface dermatitis) and LE-nonspecific disease (lacking histopathologic specificity). Interface dermatitis is the defining histologic hallmark of true CLE lesions. 🏰 Palace: Picture an INTERFACE (the boundary between epidermis and dermis) where LUPUS guards stand at the DOORWAY (interface dermatitis) checking every cell that tries to pass through—this is the SPECIFIC mark of true lupus skin disease.

questions.q: A 2-week-old term neonate presents with multiple 1–2 mm yellow macules clustered over the nose, cheeks, and forehead. The mother asks if this is an infection. What is the primary driver of this physiological condition?
opts: Transplacental transfer of maternal androgens stimulating sebaceous gland activity
Neonatal sebaceous gland dysplasia inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern
Bacterial colonization of the follicular ostia with Cutibacterium acnes
Excessive sweating causing miliaria crystallina with secondary lipid accumulation
questions.exp: Neonatal sebaceous gland hyperplasia is driven by transplacental maternal androgens, which stimulate fetal/neonatal sebaceous glands. Sebum production peaks during the first week (matching adult rates), then falls as maternal androgens are cleared. The condition is benign and resolves by 4–6 months without treatment.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 1] Physiological, Pigmentary and Mechanical Neonatal Lesions

questions.q: A 9-year-old immunocompetent child develops several molluscum contagiosum lesions with erythematous, eczematous halos surrounding the individual papules. The parent is concerned this represents secondary bacterial infection. Which of the following best explains the pathophysiology of this clinical finding?
opts: Secondary bacterial infection causing cellulitis and requiring systemic antibiotic therapy
A robust host immune response involving plasmacytoid dendritic cells and cytotoxic T lymphocytes, often preceding spontaneous viral clearance (Meyerson's phenomenon)
Progression to atypical giant molluscum requiring immediate immunological investigation
Viral dissemination into the dermis causing chronic granulomatous inflammation
questions.exp: The inflammatory halo around molluscum papules is termed Meyerson's phenomenon and represents a vigorous host immune response rather than bacterial superinfection. This inflammation, mediated by plasmacytoid dendritic cells and cytotoxic T lymphocytes, typically indicates impending spontaneous resolution and viral clearance in immunocompetent hosts.
questions.mnemonic: 🏰 Palace: A KNIGHT (immune system) raises a FLAMING RED HALO (inflammatory ring) around the ENEMY FORTRESS (molluscum) as a VICTORY BANNER before storming the castle to WIN and CLEAR the infection — inflammation = immunity winning, not infection losing.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with a solitary, indurated, well-demarcated ulcer on his penis. The ulcer is painless and has a clean, punched-out appearance. RPR is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Chancroid caused by Haemophilus ducreyi
Primary syphilis (chancre) caused by Treponema pallidum
Donovanosis caused by Klebsiella granulomatis
Genital herpes caused by HSV-2
questions.exp: The primary chancre of syphilis classically presents as a solitary, indurated, painless ulcer with a clean appearance, and a positive RPR confirms the diagnosis. Chancroid presents with ragged, undermined edges and purulent exudate; donovanosis is beefy-red and slowly progressive; and HSV presents with painful vesicles.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: A CHANCELLOR (chancre) sits PAINLESSLY on a GOLD-INDUCED throne in the castle, while HERPES KNIGHTS scream in PAIN below in the dungeon.

questions.q: Urea enhances the percutaneous absorption of topical corticosteroids and other agents. Which molecular property of urea is primarily responsible for this effect?
opts: Its keratolytic ability to denature proteins in the stratum corneum
Its bipolar structure allowing ionic interactions and incorporation into the cornified layer
Its antimicrobial action against skin flora
Its high water vapor pressure preventing evaporation
questions.exp: Urea's bipolar molecular structure enables it to form ionic interactions with salt solutions and incorporate itself into the cornified layer by breaking hydrogen bonds, thereby disrupting the skin barrier and enhancing drug penetration. This is distinct from its keratolytic effect—the barrier disruption is the mechanism for absorption enhancement. 🏰 Palace: Imagine BIPOLAR UREA TWINS (+ and − charges) holding hands at the CASTLE GATE (stratum corneum), prying open the doors to let CORTICOSTEROID MESSENGERS march through into the kingdom.

questions.q: A 28-year-old patient with non-segmental vitiligo affecting 35% of body surface area requests surgical grafting. Disease has been stable for 18 months on topical corticosteroids and phototherapy, with VIDA score of −1. Which factor remains an absolute contraindication to surgery in this case?
opts: VIDA score of −1 indicating spontaneous repigmentation
Age greater than 25 years
Extensive disease involving >30% body surface area
Concurrent use of topical corticosteroids
questions.exp: Extensive disease involving >30% of body surface area is listed as a relative/clinical contraindication because surgery is highly impractical and time-consuming for non-segmental vitiligo at this extent. Such large BSA involvement also indicates an immunologically unstable patient, making surgical success unlikely despite meeting other stability criteria. The other parameters (VIDA ≤0, age, medications) are either favorable or not contraindications.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with a photosensitive annular eruption on sun-exposed areas with minimal systemic symptoms. Which CLE subtype is MOST likely, and what is its predominant autoantibody association?
opts: ACLE; anti-Sm and anti-dsDNA antibodies
SCLE; anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies
CCLE/DLE; anti-centromere and anti-nucleolar antibodies
Bullous LE; anti-BP180 antibodies
questions.exp: Subacute Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus (SCLE) presents as annular/polycyclic or papulosquamous eruptions on sun-exposed areas and is strongly associated with anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB autoantibodies. The photosensitive nature and systemic sparing distinguish SCLE from ACLE, which shows systemic involvement. 🏰 Palace: Imagine a SUBACUT ANNULAR RING (SCLE) made of anti-Ro/SSA ROASTING FLAMES circling around the sun-exposed SKIN like a solar halo—SCLE loves the ANTI-RO/SSA duo.

questions.q: A 9-year-old boy with a history of recent streptococcal pharyngitis develops sudden onset of numerous small, drop-like erythematous papules with scales distributed across his trunk and proximal limbs. Genetic testing reveals strong HLA-Cw6 association. Which psoriasis variant is this child most likely presenting with?
opts: Plaque psoriasis (psoriasis vulgaris)
Guttate psoriasis
Palmoplantar psoriasis
Facial psoriasis with corona psoriatica
questions.exp: Guttate psoriasis is the second most common variant in childhood and is heavily triggered by streptococcal infection, presenting as small drop-like lesions rather than large plaques. It also carries the strongest association with HLA-Cw6 of all psoriasis variants. The acute onset following pharyngitis and the characteristic morphology are diagnostic.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: A GUTTER filled with tiny WATER DROPS (guttate = drop-shaped) surrounds the castle after a STREP THROAT STORM—the strongest HLA-Cw6 fortress guards are posted here.

questions.q: A 45-year-old patient presents with a 8 mm pigmented lesion on the back with irregular borders and color variation. Which biopsy technique is most appropriate?
opts: Shave biopsy for quick diagnosis
Punch biopsy to assess depth
Incisional biopsy of the lesion center
Excisional biopsy with complete removal
questions.exp: Suspected melanoma requires excisional biopsy (in toto) for complete margin assessment and accurate Breslow depth measurement. Shave and punch biopsies are contraindicated in melanoma as they compromise depth assessment and cause sampling error. Incisional biopsy leaves tumor behind and is inappropriate for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes.

questions.q: A dermatologist performing cryotherapy on a melanoma uses the principle of 'rapid freeze followed by slow thaw.' Which of the following best explains why the slow thaw phase is critical for maximizing tissue destruction?
opts: Slow thawing prevents patient discomfort and allows for better hemostasis during the procedure
Slow thawing permits recrystallization, where smaller unstable ice crystals fuse into larger destructive crystals that further tear cell membranes
Slow thawing reduces the risk of infection by allowing time for immune cell infiltration
Slow thawing enhances vascular thrombosis by prolonging platelet aggregation within the frozen tissue
questions.exp: The slow thaw phase subjects tissue to the 'solute effect' and allows recrystallization, where smaller ice crystals fuse into larger, more destructive crystals that mechanically tear cell membranes. While vascular thrombosis is a key mechanism of tissue destruction, it occurs over 24–72 hours post-treatment and is not directly enhanced by slow thawing during the procedure.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: During SLOW THAW, imagine tiny ICE CRYSTALS as SERVANTS in the castle—they huddle together into GIANT ICE GOLEMS that smash through the castle walls (cell membranes), causing maximum destruction.

questions.q: A full-term neonate appears healthy at birth. At 4 weeks of age, the infant develops fever, irritability, and a stiff neck. The parents report no skin rash. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis confirms bacterial meningitis. Which clinical feature best distinguishes this late-onset neonatal listeriosis from the early-onset form?
opts: Presence of petechiae and purpura on the skin at birth
CNS involvement with meningitis and absence of skin manifestations; symptom onset weeks after birth
Acquisition of infection via meconium aspiration in utero
Miliary granulomas and microabscesses visible on skin biopsy
questions.exp: Late-onset neonatal listeriosis is acquired postnatally or during passage through an infected birth canal, presents weeks after birth in otherwise healthy full-term infants, and primarily affects the CNS with meningitis or meningoencephalitis. Crucially, the skin is generally not involved in the initial presentation, contrasting sharply with the early-onset form (granulomatosis infantiseptica), which presents at birth with characteristic cutaneous pustules.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: In the castle's LATE-NIGHT WING (late-onset), a HEALTHY FULL-TERM PRINCE sleeps peacefully at birth, then WEEKS LATER the BRAIN TOWER LOCKS DOWN with MENINGITIS—but the SKIN BALLROOM stays SPOTLESS (no rash), unlike the EARLY-MORNING WING where grey pustules BLOOM like diseased flowers at birth.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman is scheduled for dermal filler injection. To reduce injection pain, you decide to buffer the lidocaine with epinephrine. What is the correct ratio of sodium bicarbonate to lidocaine solution?
opts: 1 mL of 8.4% sodium bicarbonate to 9–10 mL of lidocaine with epinephrine
2 mL of 8.4% sodium bicarbonate to 8 mL of lidocaine with epinephrine
1 mL of 4.2% sodium bicarbonate to 9 mL of lidocaine with epinephrine
0.5 mL of 8.4% sodium bicarbonate to 10 mL of lidocaine with epinephrine
questions.exp: Adding 1 mL of 8.4% sodium bicarbonate to 9 or 10 mL of lidocaine with epinephrine neutralizes the acidic pH (3.5–5.5) to a physiologic level (~7.0–8.0), significantly reducing the burning sensation and accelerating onset of action. This buffering increases the un-ionized, lipid-soluble fraction of the local anesthetic.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Imagine walking into a CASTLE with 1 BICYCLE (1 mL bicarb) entering through 9–10 LARGE DOORS (9–10 mL lidocaine), neutralizing the ACIDIC DRAGON FIRE at the entrance—no more burning stings!
